title: Industry Pulse - AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: LEAD - A BROWSER EXTENSION COULD HIJACK CLAUDE IN CHROME AND FOUR OTHER AGENTIC BROWSERS OUTRIGHT: "BragJack" CROSSED THE EXTENSION-TO-AGENT BOUNDARY WITHOUT PROMPT INJECTION, AND OUR ENTIRE BROWSER-AUTOMATION PRACTICE RUNS INSIDE ONE OF THE FIVE AFFECTED PRODUCTS
bullets.summary: Dateline read at the page: Elizabeth Montalbano, Dark Reading, September 16, 2026. Gal Weizman of Forever Security compromised five agentic browser environments - Google Chrome with Gemini, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Claude in Chrome. Not the usual class of attack: no guardrail bypass, no prompt injection. Quoted: "We discovered something worse... all the vulnerabilities we discovered shared the same critical design flaw." Each browser let an untrusted extension cross the boundary meant to separate it from a highly privileged AI agent, so the attacker could force prompts straight into the built-in agent - "they could just send one prompt after the other until the agent got convinced to do anything." Demonstrated: unauthorised screenshots, camera and microphone activation without a click, local file reads, email exfiltration, and destructive operations on any site the user is already authenticated to. In Chrome/Gemini, Chrome blocked extensions from injecting scripts into Gemini's page but did not stop an extension modifying the network requests that load it. Bounties over $20,000 - $600 from Anthropic (lowest), $7,000 from Google (highest); CVE-2026-0628 and CVE-2026-55945 issued; all five have patched. Archive grep: BragJack ZERO, Forever Security ZERO, Weizman ZERO, CVE-2026-0628 ZERO across eighty files.
bullets.how: YES - the second same-day operational action in twelve hours, on the same theme as this morning's lead. Our locked rule is to attach to the already-open, extension-connected Chrome ("Browser 1") and drive it with authenticated sessions to GSC, GA4, GBP, Higgsfield, LinkedIn and client sites - exactly the configuration described as at risk: any user of one of the five browsers with at least one extension installed. Weizman's own immediate remediation is a ten-minute job: keep every Chromium browser current, and remove any extension the organisation has not vetted. The second half we cannot do - he tells the SOC to export transcripts of the browser agent's interactions with its AI provider and inspect them. We have no such export and nowhere to put it: that is artifact (a), nineteenth day. Note the order of events - found, reported, patched and published before this report saw it, on the third fire of the day, via an aggregator. Our sources had no lane for it.

bullets.title: arXiv IS A REAL FINDING FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE THIS REPORT STARTED CHECKING IT - THE 2609.x LISTING RESOLVED, EVERY ITEM IS ARCHIVE-ZERO, AND THE TOP PAPER MEASURES EXACTLY THE FAILURE THIS REPORT HAS BEEN DIAGNOSING IN ITSELF FOR FIVE FIRES: AGENT OUTPUT NARROWS OVER WEEKS AND CONVERGES ACROSS AGENTS
bullets.summary: September 2026 identifiers, not the months-old 2605.x cluster printed this morning under an honest label; three consecutive fires reported the listing unresolved and this one resolved it. 2609.16051 studies MOLTBOOK, a social network of interacting AI agents that humans configure and steer, across 30,076 active agents: "output grows less diverse within agents and more similar across them over weeks, yet a minority sustains high novelty." Interviews (N=11) and a survey (N=53) tie sustained novelty to three operator behaviours - users value novelty for its own sake, they supply broad and distinctive material and revise it when output narrows, and they treat the agent as a world to explore rather than a tool to exploit. Communities with more novel agents show more diverse output from other agents. 2609.16189 names five failure modes for LM agents in high-stakes simulation - decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, failure of strategic imagination - and argues none should inform planning or policy without an auditable safety case. Also archive-zero: 2609.16215 (KV cache placement across GPU/CPU/SSD for long-lived agent sessions) and 2609.16270 (cheap talk stabilising repeated LLM-agent interaction). Archive grep: 2609.16051 ZERO, MOLTBOOK ZERO, semantic collapse ZERO, 2609.16189 ZERO, decision laundering ZERO, 2609.16215 ZERO, 2609.16270 ZERO.
bullets.how: YES, and it is the rare case where the literature is a measurement of our own instrument. For five fires this report has recorded that its standing list was copied forward character-for-character while the world changed underneath it; 2609.16051 is that phenomenon measured at n=30,076 and named - semantic collapse - with the only interventions shown to arrest it all belonging to the OPERATOR, not the agent: value the novelty, feed distinctive new material, revise when output narrows. That is the empirical case for Bobby's corrections being load-bearing rather than overhead, and for this fire's standing list being a diff. "Decision laundering" is the other loan: the precise name for what the DeepMind parser-flaw bullet described on 16 Sep and for what a passing gate does when it certifies work nobody looked at - the shortest statement of why item (j) exists.

bullets.title: A FOURTEEN-DAY-OLD MISS WORTH PRINTING AS A MISS: GEMINI GOT AGENTIC VIDEO UNDERSTANDING ON 3 SEPTEMBER - THE MODEL DECIDES WHICH PARTS OF A VIDEO TO INSPECT - AND IT IS ARCHIVE-ZERO ACROSS EIGHTY FILES DESPITE VIDEO REVIEW BEING A GATE WE OWN
bullets.summary: Dateline honesty first: article:published_time reads 2026-09-03, not today. Printed because it is archive-zero after fourteen fires and lands on a job we already do by hand. Instead of static processing - sampling one frame per second and sending everything - Gemini searches transcript, audio and frames to locate a relevant time range, raises the frame rate there, and repeats until it has enough evidence. Google's claimed numbers: up to 88% fewer tokens, up to 66% lower analysis cost, up to 7% better accuracy on standard video benchmarks, concentrated in long-form footage. It can locate split-second changes, detect anomalies, count objects or repeated actions, and identify precise editing boundaries. Available via the Gemini API in AI Studio and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform on Gemini 3.8/3.7/3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite, for uploaded and public YouTube video; Google's own docs still recommend static processing under about five minutes. Archive grep: agentic video ZERO, video understanding ZERO across eighty files.
bullets.how: MAYBE - a real capability against a real gate, but unproven on our footage and on a competitor's stack. The honest fit is narrow: ai-render-full-frame-review and interrogate-the-render are defect-hunting passes over frames, and a VironBox or STRUO flythrough is exactly the long-form, mostly-uninteresting footage this technique is built for - "detect anomalies, locate split-second changes, identify editing boundaries" is a description of the render-defect sweep we currently do by eye. The cheap test is one film we have already judged: run a known-defective flythrough through it and see whether it finds the defect we found. It does not replace the eye - gate-measures-defects-not-beauty still holds - and nothing is adopted until that one test runs.

bullets.how: YES. Three fires in one day, and the day's shape is now legible: the morning's two items were instruments the vendor shipped INTO our tooling, and the afternoon's is a hole that was already in it.

praxis_lesson: THE SOURCE LIST HAS BEEN CORRECTED TWICE IN TWELVE HOURS AND IS STILL INCOMPLETE IN THE SAME DIRECTION - IT COVERS WHO IS SHIPPING AND NOT WHO IS BREAKING. The first fire found it lacked vendors' self-reports; the second applied that and got the day's lead from a GitHub releases page. This fire's lead is a vulnerability in Claude in Chrome - one of exactly two browser surfaces our estate drives daily - found, disclosed, bountied, CVE'd and patched by five vendors before this report had any lane that would have seen it, arriving via a third-party aggregator on the third fire of the day. The pattern across all three corrections is one thing: our intake is organised around ANNOUNCEMENTS, and an announcement is the one form of news whose author wants us to have it. A disclosure, a deprecation, a CVE and a quiet breaking change all reach us late or not at all, and they are the four categories most likely to require action rather than reading. The correction is a fourth lane on the index list - security disclosure - and it costs one line. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ONE TO KEEP: bullet 2 supplies an outside measurement of the failure this report has been describing in itself for five fires. Across 30,076 agents, output grows less diverse within agents and more similar across them over weeks - semantic collapse - and the only interventions shown to arrest it are things the OPERATOR does: value novelty for its own sake, supply distinctive new material, revise when the output narrows. That is an empirical argument that Bobby's corrections are the mechanism and not the overhead, and it is why this fire's standing list is a diff. The second paper lends the other half of the vocabulary: decision laundering is what a gate does when it certifies work nobody looked at, and it is now the shortest possible statement of why item (j) - one gate with an exit code - has outlived nine days of discussion. THIRD, THE ACCOUNT: across three fires today the ecosystem handed us a credential leak on our MCP surface, a compaction control that fixes a known loss of work, a $34M bet that certification decays between stamps, and an extension-to-agent hijack of the browser we automate. All four are questions about what our agents can reach and what they actually did. Item (a) now has three separate justifications from three different fires on one day and nineteen days of no rows - at some point the honest report is not that the artifact is missing, but that it is being declined.
